# Known bugs

Open bugs, newest first. IDs (B1, B2, …) are never reused, so commits can say "fixes B1".
A fixed bug is removed in the commit that fixes it, together with a test that reproduces
it: shown failing before the fix and passing after; git history keeps the record. Finding a
bug doesn't mean fixing it at once: it is logged here and its fix scheduled with the user.
Not part of the documentation site.

**Where they live:** one file per bug, `bugs/B<n>.toml` (its title, rating, the date it was
found, whether it is only suspected, and its details in Markdown); this file is
`bugs/README.md`, and `BUGS.md` is generated from them all (`python3 scripts/bugs.py
render`; `make check` fails when it is out of date). A new bug: `python3 scripts/bugs.py new
"<title>"` writes the next number's file, to fill in, and moves `bugs/next-id` on. A fix
deletes the bug's file. The script's docstring shows a file's fields.

A bug found by reasoning but **not reproduced yet** is logged too, marked **Suspected**, with
how it would be confirmed; once a test shows it, the mark goes. If it turns out not to be a
bug, the entry is removed, saying why in the commit.


## Ratings

Every bug has three ratings, set when it is logged (by whoever finds it; Claude checks them)
and revised when more is known:

- **Severity**, what happens when it occurs: **critical** (a security hole, silent wrong
  results or wrong code run, a task run twice, the whole cluster stuck); **high** (in normal
  operation, with no mistake by the DAG's author, a task or run fails wrongly, stalls, runs on
  after a cancel, or a worker can't work); **medium** (a visible, repeatable failure that
  testing a DAG would catch, slowness growing with scale, a misleading UI or CLI); **low**
  (cosmetic, a message, a test-only flake, an author's type mistake caught at run time
  instead of at load).
- **Probability**, in a real deployment: **likely** (ordinary use or routine events),
  **possible** (a specific but plausible situation: a reconnect at the wrong moment, git-sync,
  a feature combination, scale), **rare** (unusual input, exact timing, extreme sizes, a
  hostile actor). For a security bug: how easily it is triggered, by accident or on purpose.
- **Kind**: security, data, correctness, reliability, performance, usability or tests.
  Security is a kind, not a third score: its worst case is already the severity.

**Score** = severity (critical 4, high 3, medium 2, low 1) × probability (likely 3,
possible 2, rare 1). The ranking below puts **every security bug first**, whatever its score
(the user, 2026-10-30), then the rest by score, then severity; fixes go in its order
unless the user schedules otherwise. The score is computed by the script, never written by
hand; each entry's first line in `BUGS.md` is its rating.

**What gets fixed when** (the user, 2026-10-30): every bug of severity **high or critical** is
fixed (security first, then the ranking), then features go on; a new high or critical bug
interrupts the feature work and is fixed next. Medium and low bugs wait here, fixed when a
step touches their code or the user schedules them.

## B282: a drained worker's interrupted task sometimes never ends after the worker is killed and comes back (Suspected)

- **Rating:** severity **high**, probability **rare**, reliability (score 3): `roles::a_drained_task_that_ignores_sigterm_is_interrupted_within_the_pods_grace_period` waited over 60 s for the run to end in two `make check` runs in a row on 2026-11-23 (M5.2i11, no Rust changed since M5.2i9, whose CI passed); it passed alone, 8 copies at once, the whole roles binary, and a whole `make test-integration` after. The master logged only `a queued message of a replaced stream dropped` for w1 just before the worker came back: possibly the drained worker's report dropped as a replaced stream's, leaving its attempt unresolved; the first worker's log is lost with the test (only live roles are printed).
- **Found:** 2026-11-23, by Claude, in M5.2i11's `make check` (twice; 06:29 and 06:44 UTC), the
  test failing after 75-80 s; the first run also hit B280.
- **Not yet known:** whether the master loses the drain's report (a product bug: a run stuck) or
  the test's 60 s is short under make check's load. First: the test keeping every role's log,
  the killed worker's too, so a failure shows the drain's side.

## B281: a worker's memory split leaves out its extensions' services

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **likely**, usability (score 3): a worker's heartbeat splits its memory into the agent, its fork servers, its watcher hosts and its running tasks (decision 463); an extension's service (decision 518), up to its `service_memory` each, is in none of them, so the Deployments page shows less than the worker uses.
- **Found:** 2026-11-23, by Claude, reading decision 463 against M5.2i9's diff.
- **A fix:** the services' measured memory (the supervisor measures each one every memory check)
  as one more part of the split, with M5.2i12's built-in `service_memory_bytes`.

## B280: the integration tests' Postgres runs out of connections when roles tests overlap

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **possible**, tests (score 2): `make test-integration` starts Postgres with its default `max_connections` (100) while nextest runs 12 tests at once, each roles test a master and a webserver with pools of their own; in M5.2i14's `make check` three roles tests failed with `FATAL: sorry, too many clients already` and pool timeouts, and the next run passed whole.
- **Found:** 2026-11-22, by Claude, in M5.2i14's second `make check` (the third passed: 339 of
  339). The stress target already starts its Postgres with `max_connections=500`.
- **Again:** 2026-11-23, in M5.2i11's first `make check` (one roles test).
- **A fix:** the same `-c max_connections=500` for `make test-integration`'s Postgres (and CI's),
  or a nextest group limiting the roles tests that run at once.

## B279: a worker reporting an instance the master doesn't know holds every wait_for trigger until it stops it

- **Rating:** severity **medium**, probability **rare**, security (score 2): `triggers_on_register` keeps an unknown reported trigger instance in `stopping_triggers` with an empty DAG ID, and `may_start` then holds every `@trigger(wait_for=...)` DAG until that worker reports it stopped; a compromised worker that never does stalls them all (decision 520's trust model: one worker reaches only its own).
- **Found:** 2026-11-22, by agy, in its review of M5.2i14 (its finding 4, the first half; the
  second half, another worker's slot freed, fixed in M5.2i14).
- **Why it holds everything:** after a master's restart an instance a worker still runs is known
  only by its ID, not its DAG, so the master can't tell which DAG's single trigger it is; the
  wait is right for an honest worker, which stops it at once when told.
- **A fix:** bound the wait (an unknown instance stops counting after the trigger stop grace),
  or have the worker report its instances' DAG IDs in `Register`, checked against the trigger
  records.

## B278: the remembered auth check's test needs a tenfold speed-up, which a loaded machine misses

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **possible**, tests (score 2): `a_check_that_passed_is_remembered_and_a_failed_one_is_not` (schedr-api) asserts the remembered check is ten times faster than the first bcrypt check; under `make check`'s coverage build beside the other suites it took 3.1 ms against 24 ms and failed, passing alone five times in five.
- **Found:** 2026-11-22, by Claude, in M5.2i8's `make check` (which stopped there: the rest of
  the run didn't happen). The step doesn't touch the test or `auth`.
- **A fix:** check that the second check was remembered without timing it: a count of bcrypt
  verifications the cache saved (a test-only counter), or a hash that would fail if verified
  again, as the failed one's half already does.

## B277: the metrics page's colour test checks whichever line the browser finds first

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **possible**, tests (score 2): `test_the_metrics_page_charts_each_process_with_its_tasks` reads the stroke of the page's first `svg.chart path.line` and expects series 1's dark-mode blue (`rgb(57, 135, 229)`); in a full `make test-ui` it once got another series' orange (`rgb(217, 89, 38)`), passing alone and on the next full run: which line comes first follows the standalone's own processes and when they started.
- **Found:** 2026-11-21, by Claude, running `make test-ui` for M5.2i5 (2 failed, 30 passed; the
  other failure was the new `log_levels` DAG's count, fixed). The test passed twice alone and in
  the next full run.
- **A fix:** pick the line by its series (its `s1` class, or the legend's first key) and check
  that one's stroke, not the page's first path.

## B276: the Python runner's and the extension helper's messages are typed `dict[str, Any]`

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **possible**, correctness (score 2): `schedr.runner.protocol.Channel` sends and receives `dict[str, Any]`, and `schedr.extension` (M5.2i, M5.2i5) builds and reads its messages the same way, against the rule to avoid `Any`: a message field of the wrong type passes the type checkers. `schedr.types.Json` doesn't fit as it is (it allows dates and dataclasses): replacing `Any` with it gave 78 mypy errors.
- **Found:** 2026-11-21, by Claude in M5.2i5 piece 3, adding `ExtensionChannel.metric`.
- **A fix:** a wire JSON type (`str | int | float | bool | None | list[...] | dict[str, ...]`)
  for `Channel.send`/`receive`, and typed messages (TypedDicts) for each message the helper and
  the runner build, narrowed where they are read.

## B272: a trigger's own log can't be seen: neither the UI nor the CLI shows it, only the worker's disk

- **Rating:** severity **medium**, probability **likely**, usability (score 6): an `@trigger` generator's logging (warnings, a folder missing, a key masked) goes to its attempt's log file on the worker (`/var/lib/schedr/logs/<worker>/<attempt>.log`), but a trigger belongs to no run: `schedr triggers show` gives its state, failures and last error, and nothing in the UI or the CLI leads to its log.
- **Found:** 2026-11-20, by the user in the demo: `examples/docs/event_triggers.py` now logs
  "`/tmp/schedr-incoming` is missing" once, and it could be read only with `podman exec ... grep`
  over the worker's log folder. A sensor's log is a task's attempt log, shown in its task view.
- **A fix (the user, 2026-11-20):** the trigger's log in the DAG view, for both forms (`@trigger`
  and `@trigger.poke`): the log of its current attempt, read from the worker's log endpoint as a
  task's is, with the earlier attempts' logs reachable from there; the CLI to match (`schedr
  triggers show` naming the attempt, its log by `schedr logs`).

## B270: the gauge refresh counts every run in history every 15 s, inside the master's loop: its time grows with the history kept (Suspected)

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **possible**, performance (score 2): `state_counts` (crates/schedr-db/src/reads.rs) runs `SELECT state, kind, COUNT(*) FROM runs GROUP BY state, kind`, a scan of every run kept, each `gauge_refresh` (15 s), awaited in the master's loop (`run_with`, `Wake::Refresh`), so no round starts meanwhile: with a long `[retention] runs` (or `forever`) and many runs a day, each refresh holds the rounds for longer.
- **Found:** 2026-11-20, by reading, answering "is the master operational with 300,000 runs in
  history?" (M5.2g); Codex's review of the round named the refresh as work between rounds.
  The round's own reads go through partial indexes on unfinished state (`runs_unfinished`,
  `task_instances_ready`, `attempts_open`) and don't grow with history; this one does. Not
  measured: no stress scenario starts with a filled history.
- **To confirm:** a stress scenario with, say, 300,000 finished runs stored first, then scenario
  1 on top: the refresh's time (a trace point around `refresh_gauges`) and the rounds' gap
  against an empty history.
- **A fix:** count only the unfinished runs through `runs_unfinished` and keep the finished
  ones' counts as running totals (or read them less often), or refresh the gauges in a task
  of their own, off the master's loop.

## B269: the process tests of cleanup moves, drains and cancels fail under load: one Postgres near its 100 connections, the master's lease pausing

- **Rating:** severity **medium**, probability **likely**, tests (score 6): crates/schedr/tests/roles.rs run whole in parallel on one Postgres: 0-9 of 40 fail, on the last commit as on the next (cleanup moves, SIGTERM drains, cancels; `db migrate` timing out on the pool, 'the master's lease isn't renewed in time'); connections peak at 95-98 of Postgres's 100; make check failed once on three of them.
- **Again:** 2026-11-21, `make check` on a cold build (after `cargo clean`):
  `lease::the_lease_is_renewed_while_change_notifications_wait_on_a_lock` failed ("another
  master took the lease during the switch", a 1 s lease period); alone it passed three times of
  three.
- **Found:** 2026-11-19, `make check` before the M5.2f commit: three cleanup-move tests of
  `roles.rs` timed out (`waited too long for the run to end`, a moved cleanup's handle missing),
  the master's log saying its lease wasn't renewed in time. Alone, the three pass.
- **Measured:** the whole `roles` file in parallel against one Postgres container (the
  Makefile's image): on `ce101532` 0 and 3 failures in two runs, on the M5.2f work 4, 9 and 0 in
  three; the client connections sampled each second peak at 95 (base) and 98 (M5.2f) of 100,
  means 54 and 52. One run's failure was `db migrate`: "pool timed out while waiting for an open
  connection". Not a regression of M5.2f: the same tests fail on both under the same load.
- **To look at:** each test cluster's pools (master, webserver, workers' none) against
  Postgres's `max_connections` (a test container could start with more, or the tests' pools be
  smaller); the lease pausing under CPU load (a test's lease timing against the machine).

## B265: the clock simulator's worker closes its stream at the master-time cutoff; the agent keeps it without cleanup gates

- **Rating:** severity **medium**, probability **possible**, tests (score 4): clock_sim/master.rs's alive() ends the session once master time passes the cutoff, tasks with cleanup_anywhere or not; the agent ends its stream then only with cleanup gates (cut_off_at), so the simulator never shows a stream kept open past the cutoff.
- **Found:** 2026-11-19, Codex's review of DN14 (M5.2e): a queued task kept past the cutoff on a
  stream the agent didn't close started after a late heartbeat answer, though the master had
  ended it `lost` (fixed in M5.2e: the queue goes back before the next stamp counts). The
  simulator couldn't find it: its worker closes the session at the cutoff
  (`clock_sim/master.rs`, `alive`: `past && session`), the agent only at `cut_off_at`, which is
  `None` without gates (`agent.rs`).
- **The choice (the user's):** model the agent as it is (the simulator then explores streams kept
  past the cutoff, and may find more there), or have the agent end its stream at the cutoff for
  every worker (a behaviour change: a worker cut one way re-registers instead of waiting for the
  master's word; decisions 252, 281, 445).

## B254: a worker's RUNNING count includes its wait steps, against its task slots

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **likely**, usability (score 3): `workers list` shows `9/8` running: 8 tasks and a wait step, over 8 task slots.
- **Found:** 2026-11-16, by Claude, running `examples/metrics_load.py` on `make
  standalone-separate-ui` (`WORKER_SLOTS=8`): `schedr workers list` showed `9/8` while 8 tasks
  and the run's `delay` wait step ran.
- **Why:** the count is every open attempt of the worker (`Database::workers`,
  `crates/schedr-db/src/workers.rs`: `attempts ... a.status IS NULL`), wait steps' included,
  while the slots shown are its task slots only; wait steps have their own
  (`[watchers] slots`, `watcher_slots`). Nothing is over capacity.
- **Fix:** count the two apart (the attempts don't record whether a step is a wait step: from
  the DAG version's steps, or a column), and show wait steps against `watcher_slots` beside
  the tasks, in the CLI, the API's `running` and the Workers page.

## B39: sibling groups on different layers make the run graph far too wide (partly fixed; the rest after 1.0.0, in M7)

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **possible**, usability (score 2): DAGs with many groups drawn far too wide (M7).
- **Found:** 2026-10-30, by Grok's review of M4.2b's graph layout (decision 65). A group was
  moved only on the layers holding its tasks while its box covers every layer between, so
  boxes stretched and pushed the next group further each pass: 8 sibling groups of 3 tasks
  reached tens of thousands of px.
- **Partly fixed, merged 2026-10-30** (Grok sessions `e9ee40d3`, `3b1e9c47`, reviewed by Codex
  `01a18cef`; the user merged it after a comparison with the earlier layout on 3,000 random
  grouped DAGs: 1,669 narrower by over 10%, 1,192 about the same, **139 wider** by over 10%
  (up to 2.7x, 6,000-14,000 px); the widest from 51,250 to 13,963 px; 8 / 16 flat staggered
  groups from 29,987 / 7,145,763 px to 2,992 / 5,825; layout time about the same).
  Decisions with the user,
  1 A (a group is a rigid column: its layers share the rightmost left edge, moving only right;
  a pushed item takes its outermost group along, on every layer, each item once), 5 A
  (outermost first), 7 A (a nested group whose layers don't line up is its own column; its
  parent doesn't drag a layer holding it); tests 2 A, 3 A (random trees of 1-6 groups, a
  4-deep nest, a group skipping layers), 8 B (one extra row in the random width bound). The
  original shape is fixed (8 groups: 29,987 px before, now within the side-by-side bound).
- **Open (Codex's review), for M7:** the 139 random shapes the merged layout draws wider; R1
  (high) nested staggered siblings still grow about 4x per doubling (16 parents 27,169 px, 32:
  100,629, against 7.4 million and 4.6e11 px before); R2 quadratic scans per round (`take_group`,
  `align_group`, `shift_closure`, `clear`); R3 a transitive push moves only the innermost
  group; R4 the random properties pass when no box is drawn. **Chosen, not implemented:**
  9 A (pull a nested group left of its parent's column onto it, indented; don't chase one to
  the right; push by the largest single intrusion, always the outermost group), 10 A (one
  work counter over the four scans, bound 8n), 11 A (the seven-task R3 graph), 12 B (every
  populated group has a box, plus a populated-and-empty fixed test).
- **Seen again, 2026-10-31:** `grouped_nodes_never_overlap_and_fit` found a random 13-node,
  two-deep grouping 5,830 px wide against the bound's 5,612 (seed saved in
  `crates/schedr-ui/proptest-regressions/graph/tests.txt`); the test bound now has 10% more
  room (the user), the shape stays replayed, the layout itself waits for M7.
- **Parked** (the user, 2026-10-30): back in M7, as a layout correct by construction (each
  group a block, placed recursively) plus a safety net (check, then fall back to strips),
  PLAN.md M7. It affects only how DAGs with many groups are drawn, nothing that runs; each
  review round of the repair approach found the next shape.

## B38: an edge between two tasks outside a group can be drawn through its box (after 1.0.0, in M7, with B39)

- **Rating:** severity **low**, probability **possible**, usability (score 2): an edge drawn through a group's box (M7).
- **Found:** 2026-10-30, by Grok's review of M4.2b's graph layout. On a layer a group spans
  without a task there, a task outside it is pushed right of the box on that layer only;
  the edge from it to a task on the other side is a curve between the two, through the box.
  Decision 65 keeps tasks out of boxes, not lines. Grok's case: `A0 -> U -> A1`, `U -> B1`,
  `A = {A0, A1}`, `B = {B0, B1}`: `U` lands right of `B`, its edges cross `B`'s box.
- **Cosmetic:** every task is in the right box. **A fix:** route such edges around boxes,
  or order layers so that it can't happen; with B39.
